opening: Lord, meet us gently today and always
body:
When reading Scripture, especially the Book of Acts and the writings of Paul, it becomes clear that even while Jesus walked among His own disciples, people struggled to understand who He was fully. Some believed immediately. Others doubted, questioned, resisted, or rejected Him altogether. This was not hidden from us in Scripture. In fact, the Bible is remarkably honest about human confusion, pride, fear, and spiritual blindness.

One important moment occurs when Paul and Barnabas speak to the Jews after many rejected the message of Christ. They boldly explain that the word of God was brought to the Jewish people first, but since many rejected it, the Gospel would now also be brought fully to the Gentiles. In Scripture, the term “Gentiles” simply means the nations outside of Israel — the rest of humanity. This connects beautifully with Psalm 98: “All the ends of the earth have seen the saving power of God.” Christians understand this as the message of salvation extending outward from Israel to the entire world.

This raises an important question. Scripture says: “All who were destined for eternal life came to believe.” Does this mean God predestines some people while excluding others?

Christians have wrestled with this question for centuries. Some believe this points to strong predestination, meaning God already chose exactly who would believe. Others understand it differently, believing that while God initiates salvation and calls humanity toward Himself, human beings still possess free will and can either accept or reject that grace.

What we do know from Scripture is this:

- God desires people to come to Him.
- Christ died for the world.
- Human beings can harden their hearts.
- Belief is not forced.

The Jewish people were God’s chosen covenant people, yet many still rejected Jesus. At the same time, many Gentiles accepted Him joyfully. This shows that being “chosen” does not mean people lose the ability to respond freely. Throughout Scripture, God calls, invites, teaches, warns, and pursues humanity, but people still make real decisions.

Another question naturally follows: why would anyone reject Jesus?

The reasons vary greatly. Some reject Him because of pride, pain, misunderstanding, fear, intellectual disagreement, bad experiences with religion, attachment to worldly things, or because they were presented with a distorted image of Christianity rather than Christ Himself. Even during Jesus’ earthly ministry, people witnessed miracles and still walked away. Scripture never hides this reality.

As history continued after the death and resurrection of Christ, different religious traditions and denominations developed. This can become confusing very quickly. Judaism, Christianity, and Islam are often called the three Abrahamic faiths because they all trace their roots back to Abraham. However, they do not teach the same things about Jesus.

Judaism does not accept Jesus as the Messiah.
Christianity proclaims Jesus as the divine Son of God, crucified and resurrected.
Islam honors Jesus as a prophet, but denies His divinity and central Christian teachings about salvation.

Within Christianity itself, many branches formed over time: Catholic, Orthodox, Protestant, Baptist, Pentecostal, Anglican, and others. These divisions developed because of disagreements about doctrine, authority, sacraments, church leadership, interpretation of Scripture, culture, politics, and history. Some divisions came from sincere attempts to preserve truth. Others came from human weakness, pride, or corruption. The New Testament itself shows that division and false teaching began appearing even during the time of the apostles.

This does not mean truth disappeared. It means humanity remains imperfect while searching for, protecting, and sometimes struggling over truth.

Many Christians, especially Catholics and Orthodox Christians, believe certain sacraments handed down from the apostles remain essential, particularly the Eucharist. Catholics believe the Eucharist is not merely symbolic, but truly the Body and Blood of Christ as taught by Jesus Himself. Other Christian groups interpret this differently. These disagreements are significant because they concern how Christians understand Christ’s presence and the teachings passed down through the early Church.

At times, the sheer number of religions and denominations can feel overwhelming. It can leave people asking: “How did we get here?” Yet beneath all of the divisions, arguments, and traditions stands one central figure: Jesus Christ.

Christianity is ultimately not centered on a denomination, political movement, culture, or personal preference. It is centered on the person of Jesus — His life, His teachings, His death, and His resurrection.

The deeper journey for every believer is not simply choosing a label, but sincerely seeking truth, remaining humble, continuing to learn, and asking God for wisdom and discernment. Human beings may divide, argue, misunderstand, and sometimes distort things, but the call of Christ remains the same: to seek God, love truth, repent, believe, and follow Him.

Faith is not about having every mystery solved perfectly. It is about continuing to seek the One who calls humanity to Himself.
